title_en: Hangzhou Mou Technology Co., Ltd. v. National Intellectual Property Administration, et al. — administrative dispute over a request for declaration of invalidity of trademark right
ruling_gist_en: 1. A domain name may be protected under the Trademark Law as a prior civil right. Its protection as a prior civil right requires satisfaction of the following conditions: (1) the registration time of the domain name is earlier than the application date of the disputed trademark; (2) the domain name has a certain degree of popularity and is known to the relevant public; (3) the domain name is identical or similar to the mark of the disputed trademark; and (4) the goods or services provided by the domain name operator are identical or similar to the goods or services for which the disputed trademark is approved for use, which is likely to cause confusion or misidentification among the relevant public. The evidence of publicity and use of the goods or services provided by the domain name operator may serve as the factual basis for determining whether the domain name has a certain degree of popularity.

full_text_en:
Hangzhou Certain Technology Co., Ltd. v. the China National Intellectual Property Administration et al. — administrative dispute over invalidation declaration of trademark rights

【Ruling Summary】

1. A domain name may be protected as a prior civil right under the Trademark Law. The protection of a domain name as a prior civil right requires satisfaction of the following conditions: (1) the domain name was registered earlier than the filing date of the disputed trademark; (2) the domain name has a certain degree of reputation and is known to the relevant public; (3) the domain name and the disputed trademark are identical or similar in sign; (4) the goods or services provided by the domain name operator are identical or similar to the goods or services for which the disputed trademark is approved for use, likely to cause confusion or mistake among the relevant public. Evidence of advertising and use in relation to the goods or services provided by the domain name operator may serve as a factual basis for determining whether the domain name has a certain degree of reputation.

2. A disputed trademark constitutes preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence, which requires satisfaction of the following conditions: (1) the prior-used trademark was used and had a certain influence before the filing date of the disputed trademark; (2) the disputed trademark and the prior-used trademark are identical or similar in sign; (3) the goods or services designated by the disputed trademark are identical or similar to the goods or services for which the prior-used trademark is used; (4) the applicant of the disputed trademark acted in subjective bad faith, knowing or should have known of the prior-used trademark and preemptively registering it.

Administrative Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2024) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 244

Reapplying Applicant (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Hangzhou Certain Technology Co., Ltd. Domicile: Binjiang District, Hangzhou City, Zhejiang Province.

Legal Representative: Wang Mou, Executive Director and General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Xia Zhize, Attorney at Beijing Rongli Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): China National Intellectual Property Administration. Domicile: Haidian District, Beijing City.

Legal Representative: Shen Mou, Director of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Mou, Examiner of the Administration.

Third Party at First Instance: Certain Co., Ltd. Domicile: Binjiang District, Hangzhou City, Zhejiang Province.

Legal Representative: Liu Mou, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Ouyang Mou, Staff Member of the Company.

Reapplying Applicant Hangzhou Certain Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Certain Technology Co., Ltd.) filed a reapplying application with this Court regarding the administrative dispute over trademark invalidation against the Respondent, the China National Intellectual Property Administration, and the Third Party at First Instance, Certain Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Certain Shareholding Company), dissatisfied with the administrative judgment No. (2023) Jing Xing Zhong No. 3987 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court. This Court, by administrative ruling No. (2024) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 238 dated June 20, 2024, decided to bring the case for retrial. This Court formed a collegial panel to hear the case, and Certain Technology Co., Ltd., the China National Intellectual Property Administration, and Certain Shareholding Company each submitted written hearing applications. The case is now concluded.

Certain Technology Co., Ltd. alleges in its reapplying application: (1) The domain name registered by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. has, through use, gained a certain influence among the relevant public, and the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes the circumstance under Article 32 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law) of "injuring another's existing prior right." (2) The sign "DataFoucs" was originally created by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. and, through use, has gained a certain influence in Class 42 services. The application for registration of the disputed trademark constitutes the circumstance under Article 32 of the Trademark Law of "preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence." (3) The original applicant of the disputed trademark, Certain Software Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Certain Software Company), had no intention to use the disputed trademark, and its application for registration violates Article 4 of the Trademark Law. Accordingly, it requests the revocation of the first-instance and second-instance judgments and the contested decision, and a judgment ordering the China National Intellectual Property Administration to make a new review decision, with the China National Intellectual Property Administration bearing the litigation costs of this case.

The China National Intellectual Property Administration submitted its opinion, stating that it agrees with the first-instance and second-instance judgments.

Certain Shareholding Company submitted its opinion, stating: (1) The disputed trademark is a trademark lawfully assigned to the Company. (2) Domain name registration does not constitute a prior right in the trademark field, and the registration of the disputed trademark does not constitute "injuring another's existing prior right." (3) The disputed trademark does not constitute "preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence." (4) Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s claim that the original applicant of the disputed trademark, Certain Software Company, had no intention to use the disputed trademark and that its application violated Article 4 of the Trademark Law lacks legal and factual basis. (5) Certain Shareholding Company never intended or acted to sell the disputed trademark, and has actually used the trademark. Accordingly, it requests the rejection of Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s reapplying application.

Certain Technology Co., Ltd. claimed in its first-instance lawsuit: (1) The domain name registered by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. has, through use, gained a certain influence, and the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes the provision of "injuring another's existing prior right." (2) The registration of the disputed trademark constitutes preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence. (3) The original applicant of the disputed trademark, Certain Software Company, had no intent to use it, and its application violated Article 4 of the Trademark Law. Accordingly, it requests the court to revoke the contested decision and order the China National Intellectual Property Administration to make a new decision.

The Beijing Intellectual Property Court (hereinafter referred to as the first-instance court) found the following facts:

I. The Disputed Trademark

1. Registrant: Certain Software Company.

2. Registration number: 39****63.

3. Filing date: July 18, 2019.

4. Term of validity until: May 13, 2030.

5. Sign: DataFocus

6. Approved services (Class 42): Web server rental; provision of internet search engines; computer programming; computer software design; computer software maintenance, etc.

II. Contested Decision: No. 79496 of Commercial Assessment Zi [2021], "Decision on Request for Declaration of Invalidity of Trademark No. 39****63 'DataFocus.'"

Date of contested decision: March 25, 2021.

The China National Intellectual Property Administration determined that the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate Article 32, Article 10, paragraph 1, subparagraphs 7 and 8, or Article 4 of the Trademark Law, and ruled: the disputed trademark shall be maintained.

The first-instance court found that Certain Software Company transferred the disputed trademark to Certain Shareholding Company on August 6, 2020.

The first-instance court held that although the evidence submitted by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. could prove that domain names such as "datafocus.io" and "datafocus.ai" had been registered and used, it was difficult to prove that the said domain names had a certain influence before the filing date of the disputed trademark. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the provision on prior rights under Article 32 of the Trademark Law. Regarding Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s claim of "preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence," the condition for such a claim is that the prior-used trademark had a certain degree of popularity through use. The evidence submitted by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. was weak in probative force and did not meet that standard of proof. Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s claim that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Article 4 of the Trademark Law lacked factual basis. The first-instance court rendered judgment: dismissing the claims of Certain Technology Co., Ltd.

Certain Technology Co., Ltd., dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the second-instance court).

The second-instance court held that Certain Technology Co., Ltd. claimed that the disputed trademark infringed its prior rights in the domain name. According to the facts found, although Certain Technology Co., Ltd. had registered and used domain names such as "datafocus.ai," the product materials, WeChat public account articles, sales contracts, notarized documents, and other evidence submitted by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. were insufficient to prove that the said domain names had, through use and publicity, acquired a certain degree of repute before the filing date of the disputed trademark, making it difficult to find that the registration and use of the disputed trademark would easily lead the relevant public to associate it with Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s domain name, thereby causing confusion or mistake as to the source of services. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the provision on prior rights under Article 32 of the Trademark Law. The evidence submitted by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. was also insufficient to prove that, before the filing date of the disputed trademark, the sign "datafocus" of Certain Technology Co., Ltd. had, through extensive publicity and use, acquired a certain degree of repute and influence in services such as computer software design. Thus, the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the provision under Article 32 of the Trademark Law prohibiting "preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence." Whether the sign of the disputed trademark was originally created by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. does not affect the determination of whether the disputed trademark should be approved for registration. Furthermore, the evidence submitted by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. could not prove that Certain Software Company had applied for registration of the disputed trademark in bad faith without the intention to use it. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the provisions of Article 4 of the Trademark Law. The second-instance court rendered judgment: dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

During the retrial stage, Certain Technology Co., Ltd. submitted the following evidence to this Court:

1. Information of Trademark No. 66****63, intended to prove that Certain Shareholding Company's re-application for registration of "DataFoucs" on August 1, 2022, was rejected.

2. Screenshots of Baidu search for "datafocus," intended to prove that a search for "datafocus" displayed only information related to Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s "datafocus."

3. International Domain Name Registration Certificate, intended to prove that the datafocus.ai domain was registered on July 5, 2017, and is still within the validity period.

4. Web pages about datafocus.ai and datafocus.io from the internet, intended to prove the usage of datafocus.ai and datafocus.io domain names.

5. Explanation regarding the datafocus.ai domain name, intended to prove that Wang Mou authorized Certain Technology Co., Ltd. to use the datafocus.ai and other domain names he purchased.

6. "Explanation on Certain Shareholding Company's Proposal to Sell the Datafocus Trademark to Certain Technology Co., Ltd." and audio recording, intended to prove that after the first-instance trial, Certain Shareholding Company intended to sell the disputed trademark to Certain Technology Co., Ltd.

7. Notice of Acceptance of Application for Revocation of a Registered Trademark for Non-Use for Three Consecutive Years, intended to prove that Certain Technology Co., Ltd. applied to revoke the disputed trademark and the China National Intellectual Property Administration has accepted it.

The China National Intellectual Property Administration, in its cross-examination, stated that it recognizes the authenticity, legality, and relevance of Evidence 1-4, but does not recognize the purpose of proof. Certain Shareholding Company, in its cross-examination, stated that it recognizes the authenticity, legality, and relevance of Evidence 1-4, but does not recognize the purpose of proof. It does not recognize the authenticity of Evidence 6. Evidence 7 does not affect the validity of the disputed trademark, nor does it affect Certain Shareholding Company's lawful use of the trademark. This Court finds that the authenticity and legality of Evidence 1-4 are recognized, and the relevance and purpose of proof will be discussed in conjunction with the issues in dispute. Wang Mou is the legal representative of Certain Technology Co., Ltd. and also the registrant of the datafocus.ai domain name. In the absence of contrary evidence, the authenticity of Evidence 5 is recognized. The source of Evidence 6 is unclear, and Certain Shareholding Company does not recognize it; its authenticity is not recognized. The authenticity and legality of Evidence 7 are recognized, but the disputed trademark remains a valid trademark.

During the retrial stage, Certain Shareholding Company submitted the following evidence to this Court:

Evidence 1. "DATAFOCUS (Unified Information Cloud)" sales contract and its invoice, intended to prove that Certain Shareholding Company used the disputed trademark as the product name for Unified Information Cloud and has entered into a sales contract with a third party for effective use.

Evidence 2-4. WeChat public account promotional articles by Certain Shareholding Company: "It, Over a Dozen Financial Institutions Are Using It," "China Data Valley! Heng Mou Was Among the First Selected!," "This World-Class Forum, Heng Mou Appeared!", intended to prove that Certain Shareholding Company launched products such as the Unified Information Cloud service Datafocus.

Certain Technology Co., Ltd., in its cross-examination, stated that Evidence 1 is a copy, the authenticity cannot be confirmed, and its relevance and purpose of proof are not recognized; as for Evidence 2-4, the articles published on the WeChat public account are self-created materials by Certain Shareholding Company, the authenticity cannot be confirmed, and whether the publication time is authentic cannot be confirmed, and the articles do not show the use of the Datafocus trademark. The China National Intellectual Property Administration did not submit cross-examination opinions. This Court finds that whether Certain Shareholding Company used the disputed trademark is irrelevant to the issues in dispute in this case; Evidence 1 is not admitted; Evidence 2-4 are promotional articles published by Certain Shareholding Company, which do not involve the disputed trademark and are irrelevant to this case.

This Court finds upon retrial in additional:

I. Regarding the registration of the datafocus.ai domain name by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. before the filing date of the disputed trademark, and the publicity and use of "Data-Focus"

1. On July 5, 2017, Wang Mou registered the domain name datafocus.ai. Wang Mou, as the legal representative of Certain Technology Co., Ltd., authorized Certain Technology Co., Ltd. to use the domain name.

2. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, approximately 600 persons registered on the website at https://www.datafocus.ai/, including technical personnel from Shenzhen Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. and technical personnel from China Mobile.

3. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, multiple articles were published on the website https://www.datafocus.ai/, including an article dated March 11, 2019, titled "DataFocus: Self-Service Data Analysis Helps You Cross the Data Analysis Threshold"; an article dated March 5, 2019, titled "Application of DataFocus in Group Companies"; and an article dated May 3, 2018, titled "DataFocus Tutorial."

4. When searching with "datafocus" as the keyword on search engines such as Baidu, Sogou, 360, and Bing, the results displayed information related to Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s "datafocus," and many of these results were from Certain Technology Co., Ltd.'s website www.datafocus.ai, such as the "DataFocus Database" displayed on Baidu search and the "Data-Focus Tutorial — DataFocus" displayed on Sogou search.

5. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, video materials released by Certain Technology Co., Ltd. on the internet showed datafocus.ai or datafocus, for example, a live release video of Data-Focus at the World Internet Conference posted on Xigua Video on November 15, 2018, displayed the domain name datafocus.ai; Certain Technology Co., Ltd., using the account DataFocus as a certified user under the "Big Fish" platform, posted over 20 videos on "YOUKU" (Youku), involving content such as "Visual Big Screen Export" and "Formula Overlay Nesting."

6. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, Certain Technology Co., Ltd. published over a hundred articles on Sohu.com, under the account "Certain Technology Co., Ltd." or "DataFocus," such as an article published on August 6, 2018, titled "DataFocus Launches in Hangzhou: Better Than Tableau, More Than Power BI..."; and an article published on July 25, 2018, titled "DataFocus — New Definition of BI, the World's First Chinese Natural Language Data Analysis System."

7. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, Certain Technology Co., Ltd. published nearly a hundred articles on Baidu Baijiahao, under the account DataFocus, such as an article published on March 1, 2019, titled "The Standout in Data Visualization — DataFocus"; and an article published on October 30, 2018, titled "Why Doesn't DataFocus Become a Pure Natural Language Q&A Form?"

8. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, Certain Technology Co., Ltd. published over ten articles involving Data-Focus on Sina Finance Headlines, under the account "Sensitive Fatty Jun," such as an article published on July 25, 2018, titled "DataFocus — The World's First Chinese Natural Language Data Analysis System, New Definition of BI"; and an article published on July 30, 2018, titled "DataFocus Releases the World's First Chinese Natural Language Data Analysis System."

9. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, the WeChat public account with the account name DataFocus published over 70 articles, such as an article published on November 20, 2018, titled "How to Use Data Analysis to Benefit the Company"; and an article published on April 24, 2019, titled "The Data Presentation Capability of Visual Big Screens Is Surprisingly Accurate."

10. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, over ten articles involving DataFocus were published on NetEase, under the account "Fatty Jun," such as an article published on August 23, 2018, titled "Interview with DataFocus.ai Founder"; and an article published on October 16, 2018, titled "[Major News] DataFocus Releases New UI."

11. Before the filing date of the disputed trademark, over 50 articles involving DataFocus were published on Phoenix News, some displayed under the account "Fatty Jun," such as an article published on November 29, 2018, titled "Big Data Will Affect E-commerce in Five Ways in 2018"; and an article published on February 26, 2019, titled "Data-Focus Version Update, Come and Check It Out!"

II. Regarding the status of rights of the disputed trademark

On June 29, 2024, the China National Intellectual Property Administration issued Decision No. Shang Biao Che San Zi [2024] Xi Y024620, "Decision on the Application for Revocation of Registered Trademark No. 39**63 for Non-Use for Three Consecutive Years in Class 42 'DATAFOCUS'," deciding not to revoke the registered trademark No. 39**63 for Class 42 "DATAFOCUS."

Furthermore, Certain Technology Co., Ltd. confirmed during the retrial stage that Certain Software Company did not engage in a large-scale registration of software trademarks.

This Court holds that the issue in dispute in this retrial stage is whether the registration of the disputed trademark violates the provisions of Article 32 and Article 4 of the Trademark Law.

I. Whether the registration of the disputed trademark violates Article 32 of the Trademark Law

Article 32 of the Trademark Law provides: "An application for trademark registration shall not injure another's existing prior right, nor may it preemptively register a trademark already used by another and having a certain influence by improper means." This Court will analyze this separately from two aspects.

1. Whether the registration of the disputed trademark injures another's existing prior right.

(1) Whether a domain name can be protected as a prior civil right under Article 32 of the Trademark Law.

Opinion of the Court

First, Article 18 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation (hereinafter referred to as the Judicial Interpretation on Trademark Authorization and Confirmation) provides: "The prior rights referred to in Article 32 of the Trademark Law include civil rights or other legitimate rights and interests that the party enjoyed prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark. If the prior right no longer exists at the time of approval of the registration of the disputed trademark, it shall not affect the registration of the disputed trademark." According to this provision, from a temporal perspective, a "prior right" must be enjoyed before the date of application for the disputed trademark and still exist at the time of approval of registration of the disputed trademark; from a scope perspective, "prior rights" include "civil rights" and "other legitimate rights and interests that should be protected." Therefore, the civil rights and interests lawfully enjoyed by a party prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark shall be protected.

Second, Article 4 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes Involving Computer Network Domain Names provides: "When hearing domain name dispute cases, if the people's court finds that the following conditions are all met, it shall determine that the defendant's registration and use of the domain name constitutes infringement or unfair competition: (1) the civil rights and interests claimed by the plaintiff for protection are lawful and valid; (2) the defendant's domain name or its main part constitutes reproduction, imitation, translation, or transliteration of the plaintiff's well-known trademark, or is identical or similar to the plaintiff's registered trademark, domain name, etc., sufficient to cause misidentification by the relevant public; (3) the defendant has no rights or interests in the domain name or its main part, nor any正当 reason for registering or using the domain name; (4) the defendant acted in bad faith in registering or using the domain name." Article 11 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If a business operator, without authorization, uses an identification that is similar to another party's enterprise name (including abbreviations, trade names, etc.) that has certain influence, social organization name (including abbreviations, etc.), name (including pseudonym, stage name, translated name, etc.), main part of domain name, website name, webpage, etc., causing others to mistakenly believe that it is the goods of the other party or that there is a specific connection with the other party, and the party claims that it falls within the circumstances provided in items (2) and (3) of Article 6 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, the people's court shall support it." According to the above judicial interpretations, a domain name constitutes a type of civil right and interest protected by law. When a domain name was registered earlier than the date of application for the disputed trademark, it may be protected as a prior civil right and interest under Article 32 of the Trademark Law.

(2) Conditions for a domain name to be protected under the Trademark Law as a prior civil right and interest.

When protecting the right to name, trade name rights, work title, and character name as "prior rights" under Article 32 of the Trademark Law, the Judicial Interpretation on Trademark Authorization and Confirmation clearly stipulates that certain conditions must be met for these rights or interests to obtain protection. For example, trade names need to have a certain degree of popularity, and work titles and character names in works need to have a relatively high degree of popularity. This court holds that for a domain name to serve as a prior civil right and interest under Article 32 of the Trademark Law, only when the domain name is registered earlier and has a certain degree of popularity can the relevant public establish a certain connection between the domain name and specific goods or services. On this basis, if the goods or services corresponding to the domain name are similar to the goods or services for which the disputed trademark is approved for use, and the marks are similar, it may cause the relevant public to be confused as to the source of the goods or services. Therefore, a domain name can only be protected as a prior right under the Trademark Law if the following conditions are met: first, the domain name was registered earlier than the date of application for registration of the disputed trademark; second, the domain name has a certain degree of popularity; third, the domain name and the mark of the disputed trademark are identical or similar; fourth, the goods or services on which the domain name relies to gain certain influence are similar to the goods or services for which the disputed trademark is approved for use, and it is likely to cause confusion or misidentification among the relevant public.

(3) Whether the registration of the disputed trademark infringes upon the prior domain name rights and interests of the technology company.

In this case, according to the facts found by this court, prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark, Wang, the legal representative of a certain technology company, had registered the domain name "datafocus.ai" and authorized the technology company to use it. The main part of this domain name is identical to the English letters of the disputed trademark. The content indicated on the website to which the domain name points involves data analysis, software applications, etc. The services involved are related to the services approved for use of the disputed trademark, such as "computer programming; computer software design; computer software maintenance," in terms of service purpose, content, and objects, constituting similar services. Evidence submitted by the technology company at the first instance shows that prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark, approximately 600 people had registered on the "datafocus.ai" website, including technicians from companies such as Shenzhen Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. and China Mobile. Through extensive promotion by the technology company, prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark, there were numerous articles or videos concerning DataFocus on platforms such as Sohu, Baidu Baijiahao, WeChat public accounts, Phoenix News, and Sina Finance Headlines, some of which involved the "datafocus.ai" domain name. For example, a video of the DataFocus on-site press conference at the World Internet Conference Internet Light released on Xigua Video on November 15, 2018, showed the domain name "datafocus.ai," and NetEase published an article titled "Interview with the Founder of DataFocus.ai," among others. Searching for "DataFocus" as a keyword on multiple search engines such as Baidu, Sogou, and 360 yields a large amount of information related to "datafocus.ai" prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark. The above evidence can prove that, through extensive promotion and use by the technology company, the "datafocus.ai" domain name had already gained a certain degree of popularity prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark. If the disputed trademark is used on services similar to the data analysis and software application services provided by "datafocus.ai," such as "computer software design; computer software maintenance," the relevant public, applying ordinary attention, may easily believe that the relevant services originate from the same entity or that there is some affiliation between the service providers, thereby causing confusion or misidentification as to the source of the services. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark infringes upon the prior domain name rights and interests of the technology company.

2. Whether the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes preemptive registration by unfair means of a trademark that others had already used and had a certain influence.

Article 23, paragraph 1, of the Judicial Interpretation on Trademark Authorization and Confirmation provides: "If a prior user claims that a trademark applicant preemptively registered, by unfair means, a trademark that the prior user had used and had a certain influence, if the prior used trademark has already had a certain influence and the trademark applicant knew or should have known of that trademark, it may be presumed that the applicant constituted 'preemptive registration by unfair means.' However, this does not apply if the trademark applicant proves that it had no bad faith in exploiting the goodwill of the prior used trademark." According to the above provision, the application of this clause requires the simultaneous satisfaction of the following four elements: first, the unregistered trademark was used prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark and had a certain influence; second, the disputed trademark is identical or similar to the prior used unregistered trademark; third, the goods for which the disputed trademark is designated for use are identical or similar to the goods for which the prior used unregistered trademark is used; fourth, the applicant for the disputed trademark knew or should have known of the prior use of the trademark by others. The understanding of "unfair means" essentially refers to the trademark applicant's bad faith in appropriating the goodwill of a trademark previously used by others.

In this case, first, according to the evidence submitted by the technology company at the first instance, through extensive promotion by the technology company, prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark, there were a large number of articles related to the technology company's DataFocus software on platforms such as Sohu, Baidu Baijiahao, WeChat public accounts, Phoenix News, and Sina Finance Headlines. For example, "DataFocus-BI New Definition, the World's First Chinese Natural Language Data Analysis System" published on Sohu, and "The Leader in Data Visualization - DataFocus" published on Baidu Baijiahao, etc. The above evidence can prove that prior to the date of application for the disputed trademark, the technology company had used the "DataFocus" trademark on data analysis and software application services, and it had a certain degree of popularity and influence. Second, the mark of the disputed trademark is "DataFocus," which is identical in English elements to the prior used trademark "DataFocus" of the technology company. Moreover, the services approved for use of the disputed trademark, such as "computer software design; computer software maintenance," are identical or have a specific connection with the data analysis and software application services on which the technology company's "DataFocus" trademark was first used, in terms of service purpose, content, and objects, constituting similar services. Third, the technology company's prior trademark "DataFocus" had already gained a certain degree of popularity through promotion and use. As a competitor in the computer software services industry, the applicant for the disputed trademark, a certain software company, knew or should have known of the existence of this trademark but failed to reasonably avoid it. Instead, it still registered the disputed trademark, which is completely identical to that trademark, on identical or similar services. Subjectively, this is difficult to justify, and objectively, it is likely to cause confusion or misidentification among the relevant public. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes preemptive registration by unfair means of a trademark that others had already used and had a certain influence.

In summary, the first-instance judgment, the second-instance judgment, and the appealed decision erred in finding that the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate Article 32 of the Trademark Law. This court hereby corrects those findings. The technology company's ground for retrial on this issue is established, and this court supports it.

II. Whether the registration of the disputed trademark violates Article 4 of the Trademark Law

"Malicious trademark registration applications not made in good faith for the purpose of use" in Article 4, paragraph 1, of the Trademark Law refers to acts where "an applicant submits a large number of trademark registration applications not based on the needs of production or business activities, lacks a genuine intent to use, improperly occupies trademark resources, and disrupts the order of trademark registration." The "malice" in "malice not for the purpose of use" refers to the intent to apply for a large number of trademarks not for the purpose of use and to profit therefrom. In this case, the existing evidence cannot prove that the original applicant for the disputed trademark, a certain software company, was hoarding a large number of trademarks not for the purpose of use and seeking to profit therefrom. Moreover, the technology company also acknowledged that the software company did not engage in registering a large number of software trademarks. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark does not constitute the circumstance provided in Article 4 of the Trademark Law. The relevant findings of the first-instance judgment, the second-instance judgment, and the appealed decision are not improper, and this court upholds them. The technology company's ground for retrial on this issue cannot be established, and this court does not support it.

In summary, the first-instance judgment, the second-instance judgment, and the appealed decision contained errors in fact-finding and application of law with respect to the determination that the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate Article 32 of the Trademark Law. The technology company's ground for retrial on this issue is established, and this court supports its claim on this point. Pursuant to Article 32 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 18 and 23 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation, Article 89, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 119, paragraph 1 and 122 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The administrative judgment (2023) Jing Xing Zhong No. 3987 of the Beijing High People's Court is set aside;

2. The administrative judgment (2021) Jing 73 Xing Chu No. 7495 of the Beijing Intellectual Property Court is set aside;
